Philadelphia by the numbers

Who bills Philadelphia property tax and where can I pay?

The Department of Revenue bills and collects the Real Estate Tax in Philadelphia, and the Office of Property Assessment supplies the value it is based on. Owners pay once a year, with a single March 31 due date covering both the City and the School District.

  • Online: the Philadelphia Tax Center, using the property address or the OPA account number. An eCheck carries no processing charge, while debit and credit cards do.
  • By phone: (833) 913-0795.
  • By mail: check or money order payable to the City of Philadelphia, sent with the OPA account number to Department of Revenue, PO Box 8409, Philadelphia, PA 19101-8409.
  • In person: the Municipal Services Building at 1401 John F. Kennedy Blvd. (cash accepted), plus satellite offices at 7522 Castor Ave. and 2761 N. 22nd St. that take no cash. Offices open Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.

The City's rate page lists 1.3998 percent for tax year 2025. For a house assessed at $200,000 with no exemption, that works out to a $2,799.60 bill.

What happens when a Philadelphia tax bill goes unpaid?

The account moves through a fixed ladder. Charges begin the day after the March 31 deadline and grow until the City treats the balance as delinquent and can move toward foreclosure.

  • From April 1: additions of 1.5 percent a month, running to January 1.
  • January 1: a further addition of up to 15 percent, a lien in the amount of the whole delinquency, and the account is registered delinquent.
  • February 1: penalties, attorney's fees and other costs are layered on, according to the Department's warning letter.
  • Any time after that: legal action, which can end in a sheriff sale of the house at public auction.

The Department sends a Warning of Risk of Tax Foreclosure to accounts with a balance and no payment agreement. Its text says a 2026 bill left unpaid by December 31, 2026, lets the City start foreclosure, and that debt from earlier years can be pursued at any time. The notice also points owners to free housing counseling and legal help through the City's housing agencies.

How does the Owner-occupied Payment Agreement work in Philadelphia?

The Owner-occupied Payment Agreement, or OOPA, lets a homeowner who lives in the house repay old tax in monthly amounts tied to income. An owner whose name is not on the deed can qualify if a legal interest in the home can be shown, and no down payment is needed. Some low-income and senior households pay $0 a month.

OOPA tiers, shown for a one-person household
TierMonthly incomeShare of income paidInterest owed
5$0 to $1,0750 percent0 percent
4$1,076 to $2,1505 percent0 percent
3$2,151 to $3,5798 percent50 percent
2$3,580 to $5,00810 percent100 percent
1$5,009 and up10 percent100 percent

Source: City of Philadelphia OOPA program page.

Tiers 4 and 5 fold new year taxes into the agreement. Everyone else must pay each new March 31 bill in full on top of the monthly plan amount. Applicants show two forms of proof of residence, one a government photo ID, and income records such as tax returns, pay stubs or benefit letters. A household of four earning $3,100 a month, for example, pays 8 percent, or $248, and has half the accrued interest waived. A review of actual expenses is available when the tiered amount is unaffordable.

Which other City charges can become liens on a Philadelphia house?

Property tax is not the only debt that can attach to the parcel. The Department's warning letter lists several others that the City can file as liens:

  • Water and sewer charges, with questions going to the Water Revenue Bureau at (215) 685-6300.
  • Commercial trash fees, previously called refuse fees.
  • Department of Licenses and Inspections abatement invoices.
  • Nuisance and demolition fees and fines.

Water liens can be searched at water-lien.phila.gov, which reports up to 15 years of recorded liens. The page says the results do not replace a title search and may omit court costs. If the search shows a lien, a payoff request form goes to the Water Department by email.

What does the Philadelphia housing market look like in Census data?

Philadelphia covers about 134 square miles, with a July 2025 population estimate of 1,574,281. William Penn's original plan covered only the area between Vine and South Streets and the Delaware and Schuylkill Rivers, and the old districts that the 1854 consolidation absorbed, such as Southwark and Kensington, survive as neighborhood names.

  • Typical owned home value: $243,100 for 2020 through 2024.
  • Share of households that own: 51.8 percent.
  • Median gross rent: $1,397 a month, with 679,428 households averaging 2.26 people.
  • Median household income: $61,953, and 21.4 percent of residents in poverty.
  • Mean commute: 31.7 minutes.

Interstates 76, 95 and 676 serve the city, and the county's highest point, 432 feet, sits in Chestnut Hill.

Which relief programs can Philadelphia homeowners apply for?

The City runs several programs that cut a bill or spread it out, and the Tax Center has a combined application that checks eligibility for five of them at once. Owners already enrolled generally do not reapply unless the property changes hands.

  • The Homestead Exemption takes $100,000 off the taxable assessment of an owner-occupied home in 2027, and the City says most owners save about $1,399.
  • The Real Estate Tax installment plan lets seniors and income-qualified owners pay the year in monthly installments instead of one lump sum.
  • The senior and low-income freezes hold the tax at its current level even if rates or values climb.
  • The Longtime Owner Occupants Program caps the taxable value for owners of ten or more years whose assessment jumped 50 percent in a year or 75 percent over five.
  • A credit applies to the City portion for reserve and National Guard members called to active duty.

Pennsylvania's own Property Tax/Rent Rebate program for seniors and adults with disabilities does not require a City tax receipt.

How can I sell a Philadelphia house when tax is due?

The tax debt does not block a sale. The closing figure simply has to cover what the City is owed.

  1. Look up the balance on the Philadelphia Tax Center by address or OPA number.
  2. Search water-lien.phila.gov and send a water payoff form at least 30 days before settlement.
  3. Ask a housing counselor about an OOPA first if you want to stay in the home.
  4. Order a title search to catch trash fee, abatement and other liens.
  5. Budget for the 4.578 percent realty transfer tax and the deed recording fee.

A seller on a short clock can ask for a cash offer, and the title company settles the City's claim at the table.

More questions about Philadelphia, PA Property Tax Guide

Who do I call about a Philadelphia property tax balance?

The Department of Revenue. You can check a balance on the Philadelphia Tax Center or call its customer service line. Its Warning of Risk of Tax Foreclosure letter also lists the Water Revenue Bureau at (215) 685-6300 for water charges.

What if I cannot pay my Philadelphia property tax in full?

Apply for a payment agreement. An owner who lives in the house can ask for an OOPA, and owners who do not live there can request a standard agreement. Income-based programs can lower or pause payments.

Can Philadelphia take my house for unpaid property tax?

Yes, after the account becomes delinquent and a lien is filed. The City can then seek a court order to sell the house at a sheriff sale. A signed payment agreement or full payment stops the process.

Do Philadelphia penalties start on March 31?

They start April 1. Additions of 1.5 percent a month accrue from that date until January 1, when the larger delinquency charges apply.

Does the buyer or seller pay the Philadelphia tax at closing?

The seller pays what is owed through closing out of the seller's side of the settlement statement. Both parties normally split the 4.578 percent transfer tax, though the City may collect it from either.
